findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: the question asks how Messages API streaming works (SSE, not WebSockets) and when the SDK requires streaming, but the explanation describes the difference between client tools and server tools. A learner is given no correct answer to the question asked, and the answer text is false as a response to that stem.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with one about streaming, e.g.: "The Messages API streams over HTTP server-sent events (SSE), not WebSockets — you POST once with \"stream\": true (or use client.messages.stream()) and read message_start, content_block_start/delta/stop, message_delta and message_stop events; there is no WebSocket endpoint to hand a frontend. The SDKs insist on streaming for long-running requests: a non-streaming request whose expected generation time exceeds the 10-minute limit (large max_tokens, e.g. 64000 on Opus) is rejected by the SDK unless you stream, and extended-thinking/long-output work is therefore effectively streaming-only. Proxy the SSE stream to the browser instead of adding a WebSocket layer."

findings.message: The keyed option is (c) "Wait for requests to start failing after retirement", which is plainly wrong and is even refuted by its own "why" text and by the explanation; the explanation keys the Console usage export, which is option (a) (the only option with a null "why", i.e. the intended answer). The correct/incorrect flags are flipped.
findings.suggestedFix: Set "correct": true on option (a) and "correct": false on option (c), and move the existing rebuttal text into (c)'s "why" while leaving (a)'s "why" null (as it already is).

findings.message: There is no `AnthropicBedrockMantle` class in the Anthropic Python SDK; the Bedrock client shipped in `anthropic[bedrock]` is `AnthropicBedrock` (constructed with `aws_region=...`). Both the explanation and the code snippet would fail on import.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the explanation and snippet to `from anthropic import AnthropicBedrock` / `client = AnthropicBedrock(aws_region="us-east-1")`.

findings.message: The stated endpoint `https://bedrock-mantle.{region}.api.aws/anthropic/v1/messages` is not a Bedrock endpoint. Claude on Bedrock is called at `bedrock-runtime.{region}.amazonaws.com` (dual-stack: `bedrock-runtime.{region}.api.aws`) on the `/model/{modelId}/invoke` or `/invoke-with-response-stream` path, not at an `/anthropic/v1/messages` path on a `bedrock-mantle` host.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with: "requests go to https://bedrock-runtime.{region}.amazonaws.com/model/{modelId}/invoke (or /invoke-with-response-stream for streaming), with the same Messages request body as the Claude API minus the model field."

findings.message: `anthropic.claude-opus-5` is not a usable Bedrock model ID: Bedrock IDs carry a date/version suffix (e.g. `anthropic.claude-opus-4-5-20251101-v1:0`) and commonly a region/global prefix (`us.`, `eu.`, `global.`) for cross-region inference profiles.
findings.suggestedFix: Show a full example ID, e.g. `us.anthropic.claude-opus-...-v1:0`, and mention the region/`global.` prefixes used for inference profiles.

findings.message: The snippet passes `messages=msgs` but `msgs` is never defined, so the example cannot be run or copied as-is.

findings.message: The keyed option bundles two distinct remediations (CloudFront in front of the NLB, or replacing the NLB with an ALB) even though the qualifier is "LEAST amount of change" and the explanation itself says the ALB swap is the larger change; the parenthetical makes the option internally inconsistent with the qualifier.

findings.message: The stem's qualifier is "LOWEST cost", but neither the keyed answer's justification nor any distractor's "why" addresses price: every rationale is about patching, AMIs, upgrades and fleet sizing, i.e. operational overhead. On pure cost per vCPU/GB Fargate is more expensive than the EC2 launch type, and an ECS/EC2 or EKS self-managed-node fleet using Spot with scheduled or target-tracking scaling can serve the same spiky pattern at lower cost, so the keyed option does not best satisfy "LOWEST cost".
findings.suggestedFix: Change the qualifier and stem wording to the requirement the card actually tests, e.g. question: "...Which deployment handles the traffic pattern with the LEAST operational overhead?" and mcq.qualifier: "LEAST operational overhead" (optionally add "while paying only for capacity actually used").

findings.message: "Claude Fable 5.1" (claude-fable-5-1) is not a real Anthropic model; the Claude API model families are Opus, Sonnet and Haiku, and there is no "Fable" tier. The card also makes this invented model the top-of-lineup flagship at $10/$50 while pricing Opus 5 below it at $5/$25, which contradicts Anthropic's tier structure in which Opus is the most capable and most expensive family.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the "Claude Fable 5.1" entry entirely and present the lineup as Opus / Sonnet / Haiku only (e.g. Claude Opus 5 as the frontier model, Claude Sonnet 5 as the balanced model, Claude Haiku 4.5 as the fastest), with prices and IDs verified against the current Anthropic models overview and pricing pages.

findings.message: The card presents Claude Haiku 4.5 as a current, recommended model while simultaneously stating its retirement date is October 15, 2026 — only 18 days after the stated "as of 2026-09" review date — with no caveat, so a learner could be steered onto a model that is about to be retired. The companion claim "retirement is not sooner than 2027 for the 5-series" is also too vague to be checkable.
findings.suggestedFix: Either verify and correct the Haiku 4.5 retirement date against Anthropic's model deprecations page, or add an explicit note such as "Haiku 4.5 is scheduled for retirement on 2026-10-15 — migrate to the current Haiku release", and replace the vague 5-series statement with the actual published retirement dates (or state that none have been announced).

findings.message: Option b's rationale is factually wrong: max_tokens=0 is not a valid Messages API value anywhere (the minimum is 1), so it is not "rejected inside a batch" for the stated TTL reason, and there is no synchronous max_tokens=0 cache pre-warm mechanism.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite b's why as: "max_tokens must be at least 1 in any Messages API request, so this call is simply invalid; there is no max_tokens=0 pre-warm mechanism. To seed a cache you must issue a real request (for example a tiny single-request batch) and wait for it to complete."

findings.message: Option A carries its own justification ("so a new session starts from a copy of the history and the original is unchanged"), which restates the stem's requirement of keeping the JWT thread intact; a learner who has never heard of fork_session can select it purely by text matching, without knowing what the flag does.
findings.suggestedFix: Trim option A to the bare action, e.g. "Resume the session by ID with fork_session=True.", and keep the explanation of fork semantics only in the card's explanation field.

findings.message: Option D is a verbatim duplicate of the keyed option A ("Move the contract to the top of the prompt inside <document> tags and put the question as the last line"), merely prefixed with "Adopt this approach:". Two options state the same correct action, so the learner cannot pick a single answer. Option D's "why" text also describes a different option entirely (switching to a larger/1M-token context window), showing the option text was corrupted.
findings.suggestedFix: Restore option D to the distractor its rationale describes, e.g. "Switch to a model with a 1M-token context window so the whole contract fits more comfortably." (keep "correct": false and the existing why).

findings.message: Option b's rationale is factually wrong: the Messages API permits text blocks after the tool_result blocks in a user turn (tool_result blocks only have to come first), and trailing text does not produce a 400 naming an unresolved web_search tool use. The distractor therefore teaches a fabricated error behavior instead of explaining the real reason a is preferred (the extra text can steer the model away from completing the deferred search).
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite b's why as: "tool_result blocks must come first in the user turn, but extra narration after them is unnecessary and can redirect the model away from the deferred search; the reliable pattern is tool_result blocks only."

findings.message: Option c's why asserts a verbatim API error string ("but no web_search tool was provided") that does not match Anthropic's documented 400 message for a missing server-tool definition; quoting an invented exact error text is a verifiable inaccuracy learners may memorize.
findings.suggestedFix: Drop the quoted error text: "The pending server tool must still be declared in tools on the follow-up request; removing web_search causes a 400 because the conversation contains an unresolved web_search server_tool_use."

findings.message: The stem ends with "Hint: the correct option begins \"Create a CloudFormation StackSet with service-managed permissions from the management ...\"", which names the keyed answer outright so the learner needs no knowledge of StackSets, drift detection or the alternatives to answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the entire "Hint: ..." sentence from the question stem so the learner must reason about the options.

findings.suggestedFix: Replace option C with a more tempting but still wrong choice, e.g. "Use AWS Control Tower account factory customizations only, without CloudFormation StackSets, and rely on manual reviews to spot changed resources."

findings.message: The stem's own enumeration of the pipeline stages ("extract, draft, review, refine, format") hands over the second half of the answer: the keyed "most common chain" is exactly draft → review → refine, so a learner can read it off the stem without knowing the self-correction pattern.

findings.message: The explanation attributes "native subagent orchestration" to the models themselves; subagent spawning/orchestration is a harness feature (Claude Code / the Agent SDK's tools), not something the model does natively through the plain Messages API, which is the context the card describes.

findings.message: Option d's rationale opens with the garbled label "Real technical error variable:", which reads as leftover authoring metadata rather than explanation and does not parse as English.

findings.message: The stem ("Which factors decide, and what does each option give up?") sets no scope, but the keyed answer requires roughly a dozen specific facts (exact deployment types, HTTP 400 behaviour, exact web tool version strings, billing unit, missing APIs, missing rate-limit headers). Name the two main trade-offs that decide between them (data residency and feature/model availability), and name two capabilities 'Hosted on Azure' rejects." findings.message: realWorldUsage contradicts/omits part of the explanation's trade-off: it says to add a Hosted on Anthropic deployment "only for the specific workload that needs Files or code execution", yet the explanation also lists Agent Skills, programmatic tool calling, newer web tool versions, and broader model availability as Hosted-on-Anthropic-only reasons.

findings.message: Option c's text is a verbatim duplicate of the keyed option a (CloudFront + origin access control + price class), merely prefixed with "Proceed as follows:", so two options are equally correct and the learner cannot pick one; its "why" instead rebuts an AWS Global Accelerator answer that is missing from the option list.

findings.message: The explanation states Rekognition detects "printed and handwritten text". Rekognition's DetectText is scene-text detection (signs, product names, plates) and does not support handwriting; handwritten text extraction is an Amazon Textract capability — which is exactly the discriminator this card is trying to teach in its final sentence.
findings.suggestedFix: Change "printed and handwritten text" to "text in scenes (signs, product labels, license plates)" and, if desired, add "handwriting and forms/tables are Textract" to the contrast sentence.

findings.message: The explanation's closing rundown dismisses an option that does not exist on the card: "DynamoDB is the wrong data model for PL/SQL-heavy OLTP" — there is no DynamoDB option (options are Aurora PostgreSQL via SCT+DMS, RDS for Oracle BYOL, Aurora MySQL, and DMS alone). This leftover text will confuse learners into thinking an option is missing.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete "and DynamoDB is the wrong data model for PL/SQL-heavy OLTP" from the explanation (or add a DynamoDB distractor if one was intended).

findings.message: The card asks "what controls who can trigger one?", but the accompanying code snippet already shows `disable-model-invocation: true` in the frontmatter, which is exactly the keyed answer to that half of the question. A learner can answer without knowing the mechanism.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the `disable-model-invocation: true` line from the snippet (or replace it with a placeholder such as `# <invocation-control field?>`) so the learner must supply the field name from memory.

findings.message: In the snippet, `allowed-tools: Bash(git tag *) Bash(gh release *)` uses space separation; Claude Code expects a comma-separated list of tool patterns, so the example as written would not parse into two permissions.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to `allowed-tools: Bash(git tag *), Bash(gh release *)`.

findings.message: The explanation states the description is "truncated at 1,536 characters together with when_to_use", but SKILL.md frontmatter in Claude Code uses `name` and `description` (plus optional `allowed-tools`); there is no `when_to_use` key, so naming it teaches an incorrect field.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "at startup only the skill's name and description load (the description is capped, so keep it short); the full body enters context when..." and drop the `when_to_use` reference.

findings.message: The explanation cites the Athena pricing example as showing "a 3x saving from compression and 4x from reading one column". The AWS Athena pricing example uses a table of three equally sized columns, so the columnar saving in that example is ~3x (reading 1 of 3 columns), not 4x; the specific figure is not verifiable as stated.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to avoid the unverifiable figure, e.g. "the Athena pricing example shows roughly 3x savings from GZIP compression and a further ~3x from reading only one of three columns" — or drop the numbers and say "compression plus columnar reads can cut scanned bytes by an order of magnitude."

findings.message: The explanation states Lambda scales CPU with memory "across 128 MB to 3,008 MB"; the 3,008 MB ceiling was raised to 10,240 MB (with up to ~6 vCPUs) in December 2020, so this memory range is no longer accurate as of the review date.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to: "Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to memory across 128 MB to 10,240 MB, with a full vCPU at about 1,769 MB and up to roughly 6 vCPUs at the maximum."

findings.message: The answer states that name, description, and input_schema are the three *required* fields of a user-defined tool. In the Messages API custom tool schema only `name` and `input_schema` are required; `description` is optional (though strongly recommended), so a learner is taught a false requirement.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "A custom tool definition has three core fields: name (required, must match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$), input_schema (required JSON Schema object for the parameters), and description (optional but strongly recommended plain text explaining what the tool does, when to use it, and how it behaves)." Adjust the stem to "three core fields" instead of "three required fields."

findings.message: The code snippet shown with the card literally lists `name`, `description`, `input_schema`, and `input_examples`, so the first part of the stem ("What are the three required fields...") can be read straight off the snippet without any knowledge of the tool schema.
findings.suggestedFix: Either remove the code snippet from the question side (reveal it only with the explanation), or replace the field names in the snippet with a partially redacted example (e.g. show only the input_examples array) so the learner must recall the field set.

findings.message: The stated organization storage cap is wrong: the Anthropic Files API documents a total storage limit of 100 GB per organization, not 1 TB (the 500 MB per-file limit is correct).
findings.suggestedFix: Change "500 MB per file and 1 TB per organization" to "500 MB per file and 100 GB total storage per organization".

findings.message: The Files API has no `expires_in_seconds` upload parameter or 3,600–7,776,000 second expiry window; uploaded files persist until explicitly deleted via DELETE /v1/files/{file_id}. Teaching an invented TTL knob will send learners looking for an option that does not exist.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace "files persist until deleted or until an optional expires_in_seconds (3,600 to 7,776,000 seconds) elapses" with "files persist until you delete them with DELETE /v1/files/{file_id}; there is no automatic expiration".

findings.message: The code comment "# store server-side, keyed to your tenant and user" states the card's main answer (keep file IDs server-side and map them to your own users), so a learner can answer without knowing anything about Files API scoping.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the comment to something neutral, e.g. "# uploaded.id identifies the file for later requests".

findings.message: The snippet calls `client.files.upload(...)`, but the Files API is a beta feature reached through the beta namespace and requires the beta header, so the code as written would not run.
findings.suggestedFix: Use `client.beta.files.upload(file=("contract.pdf", open(path, "rb"), "application/pdf"))` and note the required `anthropic-beta: files-api-2025-04-14` header.

findings.message: The keyed answer (option b, duplicate the stack in a second Region with Route 53 failover) is wrong and directly contradicts the card's own explanation and the option's own "why" text, which both say multi-Region doubles cost and solves a Regional outage rather than the loss of one AZ. The correct, MOST cost-effective answer is option a (add subnets in additional Availability Zones to the Auto Scaling group and enable those zones on the ALB).
findings.suggestedFix: Flip the keying: set option a "correct": true and option b "correct": false, keeping option b's existing "why" as its rejection rationale.

findings.message: Option a has "why": null. Under the corrected keying it becomes the keyed answer (so null is acceptable), but as the card currently stands option a is a non-keyed option with no explanation of why it is wrong, leaving a distractor unexplained.
findings.suggestedFix: After re-keying option a as correct, leave its "why" as null (or give a short confirmation); ensure every non-keyed option retains a populated "why".

findings.message: The explanation states ACM checks/renews DNS-validated certificates "45 days before expiry"; ACM's managed renewal process actually begins up to 60 days before expiration. The 45-day figure is when ACM starts sending renewal notification emails for email-validated certificates, so the card teaches a wrong timing fact.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to: "...for DNS validation it begins the renewal process as early as 60 days before expiry, checking that the certificate is in use by an AWS service and that the validation CNAME records still resolve in public DNS..." (and note that the 45-day mark is when renewal emails start for email-validated certificates).

findings.message: The keyed answer is option c (migrate to Aurora PostgreSQL + Aurora Global Database), but that is not the LEAST-change solution and the explanation itself states the correct answer is the cross-Region read replica; option c's own "why" text even argues it is wrong ("the largest change on the list for a problem a read replica solves"). Option a is the correct answer and is keyed false.
findings.suggestedFix: Set option a ("Create a cross-Region read replica ... in Europe (Ireland) ...") to "correct": true with "why": null, and set option c to "correct": false, keeping its existing explanation of why it is excessive change.

findings.message: Option b's rationale states that gp3 "tops out at 16,000 IOPS and 2,000 MiB/s per volume"; gp3's maximum throughput is 1,000 MiB/s per volume, so the number taught to the learner is wrong (and inconsistent with the explanation's correct 125 MiB/s baseline).
findings.suggestedFix: Change option b's why to: "gp3 tops out at 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s per volume and offers single-digit millisecond latency, so it can reach neither 120,000 IOPS nor the sub-millisecond target."

findings.message: The stem's qualifier is "MOST highly available," but neither the keyed answer nor any distractor addresses availability/resilience — all four options and the explanation reason purely about cost-efficiency and right-sizing, so the keyed answer does not satisfy the stated qualifier and the learner has no basis to choose on availability grounds.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the qualifier and stem to match the content, e.g. "Which change is the MOST cost-effective next step?" (and set mcq.qualifier to "MOST cost-effective").

findings.message: Option d references "Claude Fable 5.1" at "$10 per million input tokens" — there is no such Claude model tier (the families are Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku), so the distractor and its rationale cite an unverifiable model and price.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace "Claude Fable 5.1" with a real higher-tier model and its published input price, e.g. "Move the classifier to Claude Opus 5 ... at low effort" rephrased as an upgrade to a genuine premium tier, or drop the fabricated price claim from the "why".

findings.message: The stem's "Hint:" line is a verbatim copy of the explanation's first sentence, so it hands the learner the definitional half of the question ("What are tokens?") without requiring any of the knowledge the card tests.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the hint line entirely, or replace it with a non-answering nudge such as "Hint: consider how each model's tokenizer segments text before counting."

findings.message: The explanation pins the tokenizer change to "Claude 4.7 and later models," a version never mentioned in the stem and not one of the two models being compared (Sonnet 4.6 vs Opus 5); the mismatched version boundary makes the answer hard to verify and confusing.
findings.suggestedFix: Rephrase in terms of the models in the stem, e.g. "Opus 5 uses a newer tokenizer than Sonnet 4.6, producing roughly 30% more tokens for the same text, so counts measured on Sonnet 4.6 do not carry over."

findings.message: The explanation and option B's rationale assert a false API fact: that a non-default temperature is "rejected on 4.7 and later models" and "returns a 400 on Sonnet 5." Temperature (0–1) remains a supported Messages API parameter; the documented restrictions are that temperature and top_p cannot both be specified on recent Claude models and that temperature must be 1 when extended thinking is enabled. Option B is still wrong, but the card teaches an incorrect reason.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite both statements to the accurate reason, e.g. explanation: "Raising temperature adds sampling randomness, which makes layout drift worse, not better (and temperature cannot be combined with top_p, or must stay at 1 with extended thinking)." Option B why: "Higher temperature increases output variability, so the layout would vary more, not less; lowering temperature toward 0 would be the consistency lever, and even that is weaker than showing examples."

findings.message: AWS documentation states it can take up to 72 hours (not 72 *business* hours) to review a Direct Connect request and provision the port; the card also implies port provisioning is the main delay, when the LOA-CFA/cross-connect and carrier work are typically what stretch a Direct Connect install to weeks or months.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "AWS can take up to 72 hours to review the request and provision the port, and the LOA-CFA plus carrier cross connect typically pushes the full install to weeks or months."

findings.message: The statement that PrivateLink "publishes it through a Network Load Balancer" is incomplete: VPC endpoint services can also be fronted by a Gateway Load Balancer (and via an ALB behind an NLB), so a learner may conclude NLB is the only option.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to "publishes it through a Network Load Balancer (or a Gateway Load Balancer for appliance services)".

findings.message: The stem's qualifier "MOST cost-effective" is not the criterion that actually separates the options: every invocation costs essentially the same (one non-interactive `-p` run), and the keyed answer wins purely on enforcement/security, not cost. Option b (`--dangerously-skip-permissions`) is at least as cost-effective (fewest denials, no re-runs), so the qualifier does not select a unique answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the qualifier to match the reasoning, e.g. "Which invocation MOST reliably enforces the requirement without blocking on prompts?" and update mcq.qualifier to something like "MOST secure / best enforces the allowlist".

findings.message: The explanation lists "Fable 5.1" as a Claude model with a 200K-token window. There is no Anthropic model by that name, so the card teaches a fabricated fact.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove "Fable 5.1" and only name real models, e.g. "Current Claude models (Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) expose a 200K-token context window by default."

findings.message: Stating flatly that Sonnet has a 200K-token window ignores the long-context tier Anthropic ships for Sonnet (1M-token context window, available via the context-1m beta), so the size claim is no longer accurate as written.
findings.suggestedFix: Say "200K tokens by default, with a 1M-token long-context option available for Sonnet" instead of a flat 200K figure.

findings.message: The closing clause "Claude Opus 5, Sonnet 5 and Fable 5.1 have 200K-token windows; Haiku 4.5 has 200K" uses a contrastive semicolon but gives the same number on both sides, implying a difference that does not exist and suggesting a dropped or wrong value.
findings.suggestedFix: Merge into one statement: "Opus, Sonnet and Haiku all expose 200K-token context windows by default."

findings.message: The stem asks what you change given consumers may be offline for a week, but the explanation only says to "raise it when consumers lag" without naming the concrete change (MessageRetentionPeriod set to at least 604,800 seconds / 7 days, up to the 14-day maximum), so the answer does not fully answer the question asked.
findings.suggestedFix: Add an explicit action: "For a week-long outage, set MessageRetentionPeriod to at least 604800 seconds (7 days); the maximum is 1209600 seconds (14 days)."

findings.message: The explanation ends with "The trap is a queue attribute that lifts the body limit; none exists", which refers to a distractor option, but this is a question-and-answer card with no options (mcq is null), so the sentence is confusing as written.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword without referencing options, e.g. "Note that no queue attribute can raise the 256 KB body limit — the only supported workaround is the Extended Client Library with S3."

findings.message: The keyed answer is option C ("Attach a second virtual private gateway to the VPC"), which is factually wrong and is even refuted by its own "why" text and by the explanation: only one virtual private gateway can be attached to a VPC, and the failure was on the customer side. The design the explanation endorses (option A: a second customer gateway device plus a second VPN connection advertising the same prefixes over BGP) is marked correct:false and has a null "why".
findings.suggestedFix: Set option A to "correct": true with "why": null, and set option C to "correct": false, keeping its existing explanation of why a second virtual private gateway is not possible or helpful.

findings.message: Option d is a verbatim copy of the keyed option a with only a harmless extra sentence about recording the change in a runbook, so it is equally correct and a learner cannot choose a single answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option d with a genuinely distinct wrong approach, e.g. "Move the fleet to Spot Instances at the current m5.2xlarge size instead of committing, keeping the same capacity." — which also matches the existing "why" text.

findings.message: Option d's "why" discusses Spot Instances and interruption, which has nothing to do with the text of option d (Compute Optimizer rightsizing plus a runbook entry), so it fails to explain why that option is wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite option d (see above) so it actually proposes Spot, or rewrite its "why" to address the option's real content.

findings.message: The explanation rebuts distractors that do not exist on this card: it says "Spot reprices the wrong instance" and "consolidating onto larger instances contradicts the evidence", but no option offers Spot or consolidation.
findings.suggestedFix: Align the explanation with the four options actually presented (Compute Optimizer, buy-first, Trusted Advisor, and the revised fourth option), removing or replacing the Spot and consolidation rebuttals.

findings.message: The two keyed options restate the stem's two requirements almost verbatim ("hard ceiling on spend" -> "ends the run ... once total_cost_usd, including subagent spend, reaches the cap"; "how deep delegation can go" -> "limit how many layers of subagents can nest"), while none of the distractors mention cost or nesting at all. A learner can pick both answers by keyword matching without knowing anything about the Agent SDK settings.
findings.suggestedFix: Shorten the keyed options to the setting names only (e.g. "Set max_budget_usd on the query" and "Set CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH via the env option") and add at least one distractor that plausibly targets cost or nesting (e.g. "Set CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS to cap total spend").

findings.message: Option c's "why" is circular and does not explain the defect: it says "the docs say to set the limits as well" and "Claude Code enforces them however Claude decides to delegate" (which reads as if the prompt is enforced) instead of stating that a system-prompt instruction is advisory and not enforced by the runtime.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite c's why as: "A system-prompt instruction is only guidance the model may ignore or mis-count; nothing in the runtime enforces it, so it is not a hard ceiling on spend or nesting depth."

findings.message: The stem appends "Hint: the correct option begins \"Create a target tracking policy on a metric math expression ...\"", which identifies the keyed option verbatim so the learner never has to reason about backlog-per-instance scaling.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the entire "Hint: ..." sentence from the question stem, ending the stem at "Which scaling configuration will process the backlog MOST effectively?"

findings.message: Option b is a verbatim copy of the keyed option a with only "Record the change in the team's runbook." appended, so it is equally correct and the learner cannot pick a single answer. The explanation and option b's "why" both describe hourly manual snapshots, indicating the intended distractor text was lost.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option b's text with the intended distractor, e.g. "Take hourly manual snapshots with a Lambda function and retain them for 30 days instead of using automated backups."

findings.message: Option b's "why" explains why hourly manual snapshots fail the 5-minute RPO, which has nothing to do with the option as written (30-day retention plus PITR), so it does not explain why that option is wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: After fixing option b's text to the hourly-manual-snapshot distractor, keep the existing "why"; otherwise rewrite the "why" to match the option text.

findings.message: The explanation rebuts an option that does not exist on the card ("Tag-based ABAC in one account can scope permissions but still shares quotas and the account boundary"); no option mentions ABAC or tags, which can confuse a learner reviewing the answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the ABAC sentence, or replace it with a rebuttal of an actual distractor, e.g. "Network ACLs and security groups only filter traffic; they cannot restrict API calls, split the bill, or apply production-only guardrails."

findings.message: The explanation names the product incorrectly: it calls Quick Sight "the business intelligence feature of Amazon Quick" — the umbrella product is Amazon Quick Suite, not "Amazon Quick".
findings.suggestedFix: Change to "Use Amazon Quick Sight, the business intelligence capability of Amazon Quick Suite and the successor of Amazon QuickSight."

findings.message: Option c is a verbatim duplicate of the keyed option a (only prefixed with "Adopt this approach:"), yet it is keyed incorrect. Two options state the same correct design, so a learner cannot select a single answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option c with the Multi-AZ distractor its rationale describes, e.g. "Run the dev/test RDS instance as Multi-AZ and keep the Auto Scaling group running 24x7 so developers never wait for a restart."

findings.message: Option c's "why" argues against a Multi-AZ deployment, but option c's text never mentions Multi-AZ, so the rationale does not explain why that option is wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: After restoring a Multi-AZ option text for c, keep the existing Multi-AZ rationale; otherwise rewrite the "why" to match the option's actual content.

findings.message: Option f ("AWS Glue ETL jobs written to answer each ad hoc query") is implausible on its face — no learner would choose authoring a separate ETL job per interactive question — so it does not test any real discrimination between analytics services.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option f with a more tempting serverless-SQL alternative, e.g. "Amazon Redshift Spectrum alone, with an always-on provisioned cluster, for both the ad hoc and nightly workloads."

findings.message: Option c's text is a verbatim duplicate of the keyed correct option b (prefixed with "Proceed as follows:"), yet it is keyed false — so two options state the same correct Message Batches approach and a learner cannot pick a single answer. Option c's "why" argues against prompt caching, which the option text never mentions, confirming the intended distractor text was lost.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option c's text with the intended prompt-caching distractor it explains, e.g. "Keep the synchronous Messages API but enable prompt caching on the shared classification instructions so repeated tokens are billed at the cache-read rate."

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: it describes service accounts, OIDC federation issuers/rules, jwt-bearer token exchange and credential precedence, and never states the Files API per-file size limit, the per-organization storage limit, or any expiration mechanism. A learner is left with no correct answer to the question asked.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with the actual Files API facts, e.g.: "Files API limits: up to 500 MB per file and 100 GB of total storage per organization. Files have no automatic TTL — they persist until you delete them with DELETE /v1/files/{file_id}, so meet a 30-day retention rule by tracking created_at from GET /v1/files and deleting files older than 30 days on a schedule."

findings.message: The code snippet and realWorldUsage teach a nonexistent feature: the Files API upload endpoint accepts no expires_in_seconds parameter and file objects expose no expires_at field, so files cannot be made to "expire on their own" as the card claims.
findings.suggestedFix: Drop expires_in_seconds from the curl example (just -F "file=@evidence.pdf") and change realWorldUsage to describe explicit lifecycle management, e.g. "List files periodically and call DELETE /v1/files/{file_id} for any whose created_at is older than 30 days."

findings.message: The keyed option says "five sequential LLM calls" plus a separate programmatic totals check, but the stem's five steps already include the code-based totals validation as one of them, so only four of the steps are LLM calls. The keyed design as worded describes six steps and conflicts with the stem and with distractor c's "all five steps".
findings.suggestedFix: Reword option a to: "A prompt-chaining workflow with four sequential LLM calls (extract, classify, draft, translate) and a programmatic totals check as the gate between the first and second call." and adjust the explanation accordingly.

findings.message: Option c is a verbatim restatement of the keyed option a ("Run the container as an Amazon ECS task on AWS Fargate, started once a day by an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler cron schedule") with only the filler phrase "Proceed as follows:" prepended, so two options are equally correct and the learner cannot pick a single answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option c with the distinct distractor its rationale describes, e.g. "Launch an always-on Amazon EC2 instance and start the container from a crontab entry at 02:00."

findings.message: Option c's "why" argues against "a host you patch, monitor and pay for 24 hours a day", but the option text specifies Fargate with EventBridge Scheduler, where there is no such host; the rationale therefore does not explain why that option is wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Align the rationale with the option text after rewriting option c as an always-on EC2 + cron solution, keeping the "24/7 host for 45 minutes of work" reasoning.

findings.message: The explanation never actually explains the stem's premise (why a base model replies with more questions): it only asserts that a pretrained model "is not inherently good at answering questions or following instructions," without stating the mechanism — a base model continues the document it was given, so a question is most plausibly continued by more question-like text rather than an answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a sentence such as: "A base model only continues text, so a lone question looks like the start of a list of questions (an FAQ, a quiz) and it continues that pattern instead of answering."

findings.message: The stem's second question ("What does that say about how Claude generates text?") does not follow from the first: the base-model-vs-Claude contrast is explained by fine-tuning/RLHF, not by token-by-token generation, yet the keyed answer treats autoregressive generation as the conclusion drawn from that contrast.
findings.suggestedFix: Split the link, e.g.: "Why does a bare pretrained language model answer a question with more questions, while Claude follows instructions? And what training objective still governs how Claude emits each token of its reply?"

findings.message: The stem's "Hint:" line is a verbatim copy of the first sentence of the explanation, so it hands the learner both request-format differences (model ID in the URL path and anthropic_version moved into the body with value vertex-2023-10-16) that the card is asking them to recall; the code snippet independently shows both as well.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the "Hint:" line from the question and let the curl snippet stand as the prompt (e.g. "Given this call, name the two request-format differences vs. api.anthropic.com, how the SDK hides them, and the endpoint types available."), or replace the hint with a non-revealing cue such as "Hint: think about what moves out of the headers and body."

findings.message: The stem's "Hint:" line reproduces verbatim the entire first sentence of the explanation, handing the learner the reserved-DB-instance portion of the answer (term lengths, what is discounted, what is not) before they have to recall anything.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the hint, or replace it with a non-answer nudge such as "Hint: think about commitment-based pricing for steady workloads and about what RDS does to a stopped instance over time."

findings.message: In "take a snapshot and delete it", the pronoun "it" most naturally refers to the snapshot, which is the opposite of the intended advice (delete the DB instance and keep the snapshot).
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as "For longer gaps, take a final snapshot and delete the DB instance, then restore from the snapshot when it is needed again."

findings.message: The stem states the two requirements verbatim ("must show FedRAMP High authorization and that AWS, not Anthropic, is the sole processor of inference data"), and keyed options a and c simply restate those same two requirements. A learner with no knowledge of the Bedrock vs. Claude Platform on AWS comparison can select both answers by pattern-matching the stem.
findings.suggestedFix: Generalize the stem so it states the business situation rather than the answers, e.g.: "A public-sector contractor on AWS must deploy Claude for a US federal workload with strict third-party data-handling and government authorization constraints. Which TWO facts make Claude in Amazon Bedrock the MOST appropriate offering over Claude Platform on AWS? (Choose two.)"

findings.message: The rationale for option b asserts that "Bedrock does not accept the anthropic-beta header," which is inaccurate: Claude's Bedrock invocation body accepts an anthropic_beta field to opt into supported beta features. The option is still wrong because beta/feature availability on Bedrock lags the Claude API, not because beta opt-in is impossible.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword b's "why" to: "Bedrock exposes only the beta features AWS has enabled and follows the Bedrock release schedule, so new Claude API features do not arrive the same day; same-day beta access is a Claude Platform on AWS characteristic."

findings.message: The keyed option says to "Recreate the cache" as a replication group, but ElastiCache for Redis OSS (cluster mode disabled) lets you add read replicas and enable Multi-AZ with automatic failover on an existing single-node cluster in place; no recreation is required, so the option teaches an unnecessary operational step.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword option a to: "Add at least one read replica in a different Availability Zone to the cluster, enable Multi-AZ with automatic failover, and point the application at the primary endpoint."

findings.message: Option C's rationale states that Kinesis Data Streams "makes you size shards", but on-demand capacity mode (available since 2021) removes shard provisioning and scaling entirely, so that specific claim is no longer accurate; the valid overhead argument is consumer checkpointing/KCL management.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword option C's "why" to: "Kinesis does buffer, but even in on-demand mode you still run a consumer application with checkpointing (KCL/DynamoDB lease table) and reason about per-partition-key ordering — more to operate than a queue that a worker simply polls and deletes from for a simple work backlog."

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: the question asks what changed in extended-thinking output between model versions and what the thinking display options are, but the explanation is entirely about suppressing markdown and steering Claude toward flowing prose. A learner reading the answer would be taught nothing about thinking display and would be actively misled about what the card tests.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with an answer to the stem: describe that the newer model's thinking output is returned in a different form (e.g., summarized vs. raw/redacted thinking blocks) so a UI that only renders raw thinking text renders nothing, note that billing is on the underlying thinking tokens so cost is unchanged, and enumerate the actual supported display/thinking configuration values with a link to current docs.

findings.message: The JSON code snippet ({"thinking": {"type": "adaptive", "display": "summarized"}}) is never referenced or explained by the explanation text, and the "adaptive" type and "display" key do not correspond to any documented Messages API thinking configuration (documented shape is {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": N}), so learners may copy an invalid request body.
findings.suggestedFix: Either remove the snippet or replace it with a verified request body for the current API thinking configuration, and have the explanation walk through each field.

findings.message: The explanation's caution names "Claude Fable 5.1", which is not a real Claude model and does not match any model in the stem (Sonnet 4.6 / Sonnet 5); the model-specific advice is therefore unverifiable.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the sentence or replace "Claude Fable 5.1" with the actual model the guidance applies to (e.g., the newer Sonnet version named in the stem).

findings.message: Option (a) spells out the outcome the stem asks for ("writes one script that loops over the employees, filters, and prints only the offenders"), so a learner who knows nothing about programmatic tool calling / allowed_callers can pick it purely by matching the stem's two requirements (fewest round trips, raw data out of context); it is also the only option with implementation-level detail.
findings.suggestedFix: Trim option (a) to name the mechanism without restating the goal, e.g. "Add the code execution tool and set allowed_callers to [\"code_execution_...\"] on get_expenses." and move the loop/filter description into the explanation only.

findings.message: The wrong-option rationales begin with internal distractor-design labels ("Treats the symptom:", "Mechanism for the wrong scope:", "Real technical error variable:") that are authoring metadata, not learner-facing explanation, and they hint at how each distractor was constructed.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the leading labels and start each "why" with the substantive explanation (e.g. "Parallel calls compress 20 turns into one, but all 20 raw results still enter Claude's context...").

findings.message: The tool identifier "code_execution_20260120" does not correspond to a documented code execution tool version; programmatic tool calling with allowed_callers is documented against the published code execution tool version (code_execution_20250825), so the invented date-stamp may mislead learners copying the value.
findings.suggestedFix: Use the documented version string (e.g. code_execution_20250825) in both the option text and the allowed_callers array, or write it generically as "the code execution tool type".

findings.message: The explanation claims "one model round trip instead of 20", but programmatic tool calling still requires at least two model turns: one to emit the script and one to consume the script's returned output and produce the report.
findings.suggestedFix: Rephrase to "a single script-and-result exchange instead of 20 tool-call turns" or "roughly two model turns instead of 20".

findings.message: Option D announces its own defect in the option text ("without creating permission sets or account assignments"), so no learner needs any knowledge of Identity Center to rule it out; the option is self-defeating rather than tempting.
findings.suggestedFix: Make D a plausible-but-wrong Identity Center answer without the giveaway clause, e.g. "Enable IAM Identity Center in the management account and create permission sets for dev and prod, keeping the existing IAM users in the identity account as the sign-in identities for those accounts." and explain in the "why" that Identity Center identities are separate from the identity account's IAM users, so this does not give those users cross-account access.

findings.message: Option C's text is a verbatim copy of the keyed option A (only prefixed with "Adopt this approach:"), so two options describe the identical strategy but only A is keyed; a learner cannot pick a single correct answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option C with the distractor its rationale describes, e.g. "Wrap the streaming call in a try/except block and catch the refusal as an API exception."

findings.message: Option C's "why" ("No exception is raised: the refusal arrives as ordinary stream events, so the handler never fires") does not explain the text of option C at all, which contains no exception handling; the rationale belongs to a different distractor.
findings.suggestedFix: After rewriting option C as an exception-handling distractor, keep this rationale; otherwise rewrite the "why" to match the option text.

findings.message: The code snippet shown with the card already contains `"cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}` at the top level of the request body, which is exactly the first thing the stem asks the learner to recall ("Which request field does that"). The learner can read the answer off the snippet without knowing anything about automatic caching.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the `cache_control` line from the snippet (show only model, max_tokens, system and the growing messages array, i.e. the request the learner must modify), or move the full snippet into the explanation as the answer.

findings.message: The answer text asserts "Moving to Standard-IA at day 7 alone is valid," but S3 Lifecycle requires objects to be stored at least 30 days in the current class (S3 Standard) before transitioning to S3 Standard-IA or One Zone-IA, so a day 7 transition to Standard-IA is itself rejected. Both steps of the rule are invalid, not just the day 20 step, so the keyed reasoning teaches a false rule.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite the answer to state that S3 rejects both steps: the day 7 Standard-IA transition violates the 30-day minimum in S3 Standard before a Standard-IA/One Zone-IA transition, and the day 20 Deep Archive step violates the requirement that it be at least 30 days after the Standard-IA transition (day 60 or later if the IA step is moved to day 30). Alternatively, change the stem to move the IA transition to day 30 so the day 20 Deep Archive step is the single fault.

findings.message: The explanation's closing sentence ("The distractor blames the day 7 IA step or accepts the rule unchanged") refers to distractor options, but this is a question-and-answer card with mcq: null, so there are no options for the learner to see.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the sentence about distractors, or convert the card to an MCQ with those options actually present.

findings.message: The explanation says only "a peered VPC in another Region" is excluded from using a gateway endpoint, implying a same-Region peered VPC could reach it. Gateway endpoints cannot be reached over any VPC peering connection (or VPN/Direct Connect/transit gateway), regardless of Region.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "...traffic originating outside the VPC — an on-premises network, any peered VPC, or a transit gateway path — cannot use a gateway endpoint and needs an interface endpoint instead."

findings.message: Option c is trivially eliminable because the stem already states there is no NAT gateway, so a learner can reject it without knowing anything about aws:SourceIp and VPC endpoint traffic (the actual concept being tested).
findings.suggestedFix: Reword option c so the misconception is the tested point rather than a fact contradicted by the stem, e.g. "Add a bucket policy that allows only requests whose aws:SourceIp matches the private CIDR of the instances' subnets." and keep the "why" focused on aws:SourceIp being unavailable for gateway-endpoint traffic (aws:VpcSourceIp is the applicable key).

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: the question asks how manual extended thinking is configured and what rules budget_tokens follows, but the explanation discusses workspace-scoped file uploads, file_id isolation and per-tenant workspaces. A learner is given an unrelated (and therefore wrong) answer to the question posed.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with the actual answer, e.g.: "Set thinking: {\"type\": \"enabled\", \"budget_tokens\": N} on the Messages request. budget_tokens must be at least 1024 and must be strictly less than max_tokens; it is a target, not a hard cap on billed output, and thinking tokens count toward output tokens. Larger budgets improve quality on hard reasoning tasks with diminishing returns, and budgets above ~32k are best run with batch/streaming to avoid timeouts."

findings.message: The code snippet shows the complete answer to the first half of the stem (thinking: {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 8000} alongside max_tokens), so a learner can read off how manual extended thinking is configured without knowing it.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the thinking block from the snippet (or show only model/max_tokens/messages) so the learner must supply the thinking configuration themselves.

findings.message: The realWorldUsage cites a field that does not exist in the Anthropic Messages API response: usage reports input_tokens/output_tokens (thinking tokens are included in output_tokens); there is no usage.output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens (that shape mirrors OpenAI's completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens).
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens, so compare usage.output_tokens across runs (or sum the thinking block content) to see what a budget actually cost before raising it."

findings.message: The realWorldUsage note claims "for a brand-new VPC, a regional NAT gateway expands across zones on its own" — no such AWS resource exists. A NAT gateway is always a zonal resource created in a single subnet in one Availability Zone; there is no regional or auto-expanding NAT gateway, so this teaches a false fact that also contradicts the card's own explanation.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "NAT gateways are always zonal. Whether the VPC is new or existing, high availability requires one NAT gateway per AZ plus a per-subnet route table pointing at the same-zone gateway — the extra gateway alone is not enough."

findings.message: The explanation's final sentence ("Interface endpoints reach only AWS services, not an external API") rebuts a VPC interface endpoint option that does not exist among options a–d, so it is confusing leftover text from a different card version.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the sentence about interface endpoints, or add an interface-endpoint distractor option that the sentence actually addresses.

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: the question asks which of Lambda or Fargate runs each workload and what shortens cold starts, but the explanation describes AWS Lake Formation, the Glue Data Catalog, LF-Tags and data filters. A learner would be given entirely false information as the answer to this compute question.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with the Lambda/Fargate answer, e.g.: "Lambda for the bursty API (scales instantly per request), the S3-triggered thumbnailer (event-driven) and the 200,000-message SQS queue (batch polling with high concurrency). Fargate for the nightly 40-minute report, because Lambda's maximum execution time is 15 minutes. Cold starts are shortened by provisioned concurrency (or Lambda SnapStart for Java/.NET/Python), smaller deployment packages/fewer dependencies, and moving connection and SDK client creation outside the handler so it is reused by warm invocations."

findings.message: The stem bundles four workload placements plus an open-ended "what shortens the cold start?" into one question, and gives no criterion (cost, latency, operational overhead) or scope for the cold-start part, so many different answers (provisioned concurrency, SnapStart, smaller package, init outside handler, more memory) are all defensible.
findings.suggestedFix: Split into focused cards, and make the cold-start question specific, e.g. "Which Lambda feature keeps initialized execution environments ready so the S3-triggered thumbnailer avoids cold starts?"

findings.message: The code snippet's comment ("Created once per environment, reused by every warm invocation") and the realWorldUsage note state the cold-start remedy outright, so the learner can answer that part of the stem without knowing the material.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the explanatory comment from the snippet (show only the static NpgsqlDataSource declaration without saying why) and move the realWorldUsage wording into the explanation rather than showing it alongside the question.

findings.message: The stem's "Hint:" line is a verbatim copy of the explanation's first sentence ("Create an origin group of a primary and a secondary origin and assign it to the cache behaviour"), so it hands the learner the entire "how do you make CloudFront fall back" half of the question without requiring any knowledge of origin groups.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the hint, or replace it with a non-revealing nudge such as "Hint: think about how CloudFront can be configured with more than one origin for a single cache behaviour, and which HTTP methods and response codes are eligible."

findings.message: The per-image size limit is stated backwards: Anthropic documents a maximum of 5 MB per image for Claude API requests and 10 MB per image on claude.ai, not 10 MB on the API with 5 MB reserved for Bedrock/Vertex. A learner sizing scans to 10 MB per image would get rejections.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "each image at most 5 MB on the Claude API (10 MB on claude.ai) and 8000 by 8000 px", and drop or verify the separate Bedrock/Google Cloud parenthetical.

findings.message: The "up to 600 images (100 on models with a 200k-token context window)" figure does not match the documented per-request image cap (100 images per request on the Claude API, 20 on claude.ai); no 600-image tier is documented, so this number is unverifiable as written.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with the documented cap, e.g. "a request may include up to 100 images on the Claude API (20 on claude.ai)", or cite the specific source for any higher long-context limit.

findings.message: The explanation's final sentence rebuts an Amazon Macie option ("Macie finds sensitive data; it never authorizes access"), but no option in this card mentions Macie, so the sentence is leftover text that will confuse learners.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the sentence "Macie finds sensitive data; it never authorizes access." (or replace it with a rebuttal of option D, the nightly Glue copy).

findings.message: The keyed answer is option b (aws:SourceIp), but that option is factually wrong for the stem and the card's own explanation and option b's "why" both say so: a source-IP condition still allows direct kms:Decrypt from the office CIDR and would block S3's own requests. The correct answer is option a (kms:ViaService = s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com plus kms:CallerAccount), which is currently keyed false and has a null "why".
findings.suggestedFix: Set option a "correct": true and option b "correct": false; move the existing option b rationale into b's "why" (it already reads as a wrong-answer explanation) and leave a's "why" null as the keyed answer.

findings.message: The keyed answer is option d ("Parse the text anyway and ship it"), which is factually wrong and contradicted by both the card's own explanation and that option's own "why" text calling it "the classic swallowed failure". The correct FIRST action is option a: treat the response as truncated and enable compaction/context editing.
findings.suggestedFix: Set "correct": true on option a and "correct": false on option d. Give option a "why": null (or a brief rationale) and give option d a distractor rationale, e.g. "Consuming a truncated report as if it were complete is the classic swallowed failure: missing sections reach users with no signal that anything was cut."

findings.message: Option d repeats option a verbatim (Firehose stream with S3 destination buffering into tens-of-megabytes objects) and only adds "Record the change in the team's runbook," so it is equally correct while only a is keyed; the learner cannot pick a single answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option d with the Transfer Acceleration distractor its "why" and the explanation assume, e.g. "Keep one PutObject per reading but enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the destination bucket."

findings.message: Option d's "why" explains that S3 Transfer Acceleration does not reduce PUT counts, which has no relation to the option's actual text about Firehose buffering plus a runbook entry; the explanation likewise lists Transfer Acceleration as a rejected option that does not exist.
findings.suggestedFix: After restoring the Transfer Acceleration option text, keep the existing "why"; otherwise rewrite the "why" to address whatever distractor replaces option d.

findings.message: The qualifier "MOST cost-effective" does not discriminate among the options: the card's own explanation and realWorldUsage select option A for being the only *enforceable* control, while the cheapest/lowest-effort options are actually B (one system-prompt line) and D (a config edit). Cost is irrelevant to the hard "can never write" requirement, so the stated qualifier is not what the keyed answer best satisfies.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the qualifier and stem to target enforcement, e.g. qualifier "MOST reliable" and stem "...Which implementation MOST reliably enforces this, even in an auto-approving permission mode?"

findings.message: The explanation lists "fable" as a valid value for the agent frontmatter `model` field. Claude Code accepts the aliases `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, a full model id, or `inherit`; there is no `fable` alias, so learners would memorize a nonexistent value.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove "fable": "model can be sonnet, opus, haiku, a full model id, or inherit".

findings.message: The stem's "Hint:" line is copied verbatim from the first sentence of the explanation, so it answers two of the three things the question asks (where the definition lives and which fields are required) before the learner recalls anything.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the Hint line from the question, or replace it with a non-answering cue such as "Hint: think about file location, delegation trigger, tool scoping and context isolation."

findings.message: The stem's only stated requirements are that sessions survive instance loss/scaling and that stickiness not be used, and it adds the undefined phrase "it wants an acceptable option" instead of a decidable criterion. Options C (RDS Multi-AZ) and D (EFS) also keep sessions off the instances and survive instance loss, so nothing in the stem lets a learner exclude them; the explanation decides the question on latency, a requirement that never appears in the stem.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace "and it wants an acceptable option" with an explicit criterion, e.g. "The solution must provide sub-millisecond session lookups with minimal added latency per request."

findings.message: The explanation spends a sentence on "DynamoDB with a TTL attribute" as the serverless alternative, but DynamoDB is not one of the four options, which can make a learner think they missed an answer choice.
findings.suggestedFix: Drop the DynamoDB sentence or clearly mark it as a note about an alternative not offered here, and instead explain why ElastiCache beats the RDS and EFS options presented.

findings.message: Option d's rationale says the cost is incurred "after 25 bloated results," but the stem states a typical session runs 30 searches before the context fills; the numbers should match so learners aren't confused about the scenario.
findings.suggestedFix: Change option d's why to "...after 30 bloated results have already cost money and attention..." to match the stem.

findings.message: Option b's "why" asserts that "the documented remedy is a prompt for a fixed cadence (one consult before substantive work, one before finishing)" — a remedy that appears in no option and that contradicts the explanation's blanket claim that "a prompt plea does not restore that detection." A learner is left thinking a cadence prompt (cheaper than restoring default effort) was the real best answer but unavailable.
findings.suggestedFix: Trim b's "why" to the reason it is wrong without prescribing an off-card remedy, e.g. "A consult instruction keyed to the executor's own judgment cannot help: a low-effort executor has stopped detecting that it is stuck, so the consult rate and the underlying effort problem both remain." Or align the explanation with it if the cadence prompt is in fact the recommended fix.

findings.message: "Claude Fable 5.1" is not an Anthropic model name (the families are Haiku, Sonnet and Opus), yet it is mixed with the real-style name "Claude Sonnet 5" in the stem and in keyed option a, which makes the card look like it is teaching a nonexistent model as the stronger advisor tier.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace "Claude Fable 5.1" with the actual stronger-tier model intended (e.g. "Claude Opus 4.5"), or use an explicitly generic label such as "a frontier-tier Opus advisor" in both the stem and option a.

findings.message: The explanation (and option b's "why") cites only the first two internet egress tiers ($0.09 for the first 10 TB, $0.085 for the next 40 TB) for a 100 TB/month workload; the remaining ~50 TB falls in the $0.07/GB tier, so the quoted tiers do not cover the stated volume and overstate the marginal rate.
findings.suggestedFix: State the full tier ladder for 100 TB, e.g. "$0.09/GB for the first 10 TB, $0.085 for the next 40 TB, and $0.07 for the next 100 TB — about $8,000 a month for 100 TB, versus ~$2,050 at the Direct Connect rate of $0.02/GB."

findings.message: Option c (plain internet with TLS) is eliminable directly from the stem's explicit "the path must be private" requirement without any pricing or Direct Connect knowledge, so it adds little discrimination.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option c with a plausible private-path alternative, e.g. "A 500 Mbps hosted Direct Connect connection with no VPN backup" or "Two 500 Mbps hosted connections at separate Direct Connect locations", and explain why it is less cost-effective or less resilient.

findings.message: Option c invents a mechanism: Claude Code has no `/autocompact` slash command and the auto-compact threshold is not a user-adjustable "window" (auto-compact is only an on/off setting, with `/compact` for manual compaction), so the distractor is unrealistic as worded.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword option c to a real action, e.g. "Disable auto-compact in /config and run /compact manually so the large CLAUDE.md is summarized away," and adjust the `why` to note that compaction never changes what is loaded at session start.

findings.message: For REST APIs, a VPC link private integration can only target an internal Network Load Balancer; Application Load Balancers (and Cloud Map services) are supported only by HTTP API VPC links. The explanation's claim that a VPC link "reaches an internal NLB or ALB" is wrong for the REST API scenario in the stem, which explicitly puts the service behind an internal ALB.
findings.suggestedFix: State that a REST API VPC link targets an internal Network Load Balancer only, so an internal-ALB backend must be fronted by an NLB (or exposed through an HTTP API, whose VPC links support ALB, NLB and Cloud Map).

findings.message: The integration timeout is no longer a hard, unraisable 29-second limit: since mid-2024 AWS allows a quota increase above 29 seconds (up to 900 seconds) for Regional and private REST APIs, so "a hard limit that no API type can raise" is out of date as of the review date (HTTP APIs remain capped at 30 seconds).
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "The integration timeout defaults to 29 seconds (50 ms minimum). For Regional and private REST APIs you can request a quota increase above 29 seconds (up to 900 s), with the trade-off of long-held connections; HTTP APIs stay capped at 30 seconds. Even so, the recommended pattern for a two-minute job is to return 202 and complete asynchronously via SQS or Step Functions."

findings.message: The explanation asserts that "a Read deny also blocks Edit and Write on the same path." Claude Code's permission rules are per tool: a `Read(...)` deny rule blocks the Read tool (and recognized file-reading Bash commands), but it does not by itself deny Edit/Write/NotebookEdit on that path — which is exactly why the keyed option has to add a separate `Edit(./.env*)` rule. Teaching the opposite would lead learners to omit the Edit deny and leave writes unblocked.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "Put the prohibition in permissions.deny: deny rules take precedence over ask and allow. Rules are per tool, so you need both Read(...) rules (which also cover file-reading Bash commands such as cat) and an Edit(...) rule (which also covers Write and NotebookEdit) to block reading and modification."

findings.message: The explanation rebuts a Snowball/offline bulk transfer option ("Snowball is offline bulk transfer with no change capture..."), but no such option exists among a-d, so the explanation does not match the card's options and may confuse learners.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the Snowball sentence from the explanation (or add a Snowball-based distractor option if that rebuttal is intended to be kept).

findings.message: The realWorldUsage advice is technically wrong: for UnHealthyHostCount an early-warning alarm should use the Maximum statistic (AWS documents Maximum as the useful statistic for UnHealthyHostCount, and Minimum for HealthyHostCount). An alarm on UnHealthyHostCount Minimum > 0 fires later/less reliably than Maximum > 0, and the claim that Minimum > 0 is "the AWS-recommended early warning" is unsupported.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to: "Add a companion alarm on UnHealthyHostCount with the Maximum statistic greater than 0 for more than one data point as an early warning before the healthy count falls."

findings.message: Option c is also a valid answer as the stem is written: switching the image block to a url source keeps the image in the model's context while shrinking every request body from 6 MB of base64 to a short URL, so it fixes the latency problem too. The option's "why" disqualifies it only by appealing to confidentiality, a constraint that appears nowhere in the stem.
findings.suggestedFix: Add the missing constraint to the stem, e.g. "...exchanges 40 tool-use turns about it. The inspection photos are confidential and may not be hosted on any publicly reachable URL. Every request now carries the photo again and p95 latency has doubled..." so that only the Files API option qualifies.

findings.message: Option a is eliminated directly by the stem's own requirement ("keeps the photo in the model's context") without any knowledge of the Files API, so no learner would select it.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option a with a distractor that keeps the image available, e.g. "Re-upload the base64 image only every fifth turn and rely on the model remembering it in between," and explain in "why" that omitted image blocks are simply absent from those requests.

findings.message: The stem asks the learner to produce the `claude mcp add` commands for an HTTP server with a bearer token and for an npx stdio server, but the codeSnippet shown with the card contains those exact commands verbatim, so the learner can read off the answer without recalling the syntax.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the codeSnippet (or replace it with a blanked template such as `claude mcp add --transport ____ github ____ --header "____"` / `claude mcp add --transport ____ airtable --env ____ ____ npx -y airtable-mcp-server`) and keep the full commands only in the explanation.

findings.message: The codeSnippet shown with the stem is itself the answer: the stem asks what the reply block looks like "including for a tool that failed," and the snippet displays a user-role tool_result block with tool_use_id echoing the id and is_error set to true, so the learner needs none of the tested knowledge.
findings.suggestedFix: Move the tool_result JSON into the explanation and replace the card's codeSnippet with the assistant-side stimulus instead, e.g. a tool_use block {"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_01A09q90qw90lq917835lq9","name":"get_weather","input":{"location":"Paris"}}, and ask the learner to construct the reply.

findings.message: Option D's rationale asserts that "SSE-C has been blocked by default on new buckets since April 2026," which is not a real AWS change; SSE-C remains an available, unblocked option on S3 buckets as of the review date, so the card teaches a fabricated fact.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the clause "and SSE-C has been blocked by default on new buckets since April 2026" from option D's "why", leaving the accurate reasons (client-supplied keys, no key policy to revoke, no KMS Decrypt audit trail).

findings.message: The explanation's final sentence dismisses AWS Shield Advanced, but Shield Advanced is not one of the four options, so the rebuttal is a dangling reference that can confuse a learner comparing the explanation to the option list.
findings.suggestedFix: Drop the Shield Advanced sentence, or replace it with a rebuttal of an option that actually appears, e.g. "A blackhole route only influences where outbound packets go, so it cannot stop inbound requests."

findings.message: Option d's "why" states the Admin API accepts "an org:admin OAuth token, or a personal or service account key not scoped to a workspace"; Anthropic's Admin API (including usage_report/cost_report) requires a dedicated Admin API key (sk-ant-admin...) provisioned by an org admin, so regular personal or service-account keys are also rejected. This teaches an incorrect access model in the rationale.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite d's why as: "The Admin API rejects workspace-scoped (and ordinary) API keys; usage_report and cost_report require an Admin API key (sk-ant-admin...) provisioned by an organization admin. Filter by workspace using the workspace_id parameter or group_by instead."

findings.message: Option a says both endpoints are "grouped by workspace and model," but only usage_report supports grouping by model; cost_report's group_by is limited to workspace_id and description, so the option overstates cost_report's grouping capability.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword a as: "The Usage and Cost Admin API (usage_report grouped by workspace and model, cost_report grouped by workspace and description), called with an Admin API key."

findings.message: The claim that "role sessions (EC2, Lambda, AssumeRole) carry no MFA information, so the key reads false" is false for AssumeRole: when SerialNumber and TokenCode are passed to sts:AssumeRole (e.g. a CLI profile with mfa_serial), the resulting role session does carry aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent = true, which is exactly how MFA conditions in permission and resource policies are satisfied by human role sessions. Only sessions obtained without MFA parameters (service roles for EC2/Lambda, plain role chaining) read false.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "Service-linked/workload role sessions (EC2 instance profiles, Lambda execution roles) and role assumptions made without MFA parameters carry no MFA context, so the key reads false and an MFA Deny in an SCP blocks every workload role. A role session created by an AssumeRole call that passes SerialNumber and TokenCode does report aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent = true, so enforce MFA in the trust policy of human roles instead."

findings.message: The explanation states a Kinesis data stream retains records "24 hours by default and up to 7 days". Since long-term retention was introduced (Nov 2020), Kinesis Data Streams supports retention up to 365 days; 7 days is only the extended-retention tier, not the maximum.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "A data stream keeps records for 24 hours by default, can be extended to 7 days, and supports long-term retention up to 365 days, so 7-day replay is just a retention setting."

findings.message: The explanation says "SQS is a work queue that delivers each message once"; an SQS standard queue provides at-least-once delivery (duplicates are possible). The relevant point is that each message is delivered to one consumer and deleted, not that delivery is exactly-once.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to: "SQS is a work queue: each message is normally processed and deleted by a single consumer (standard queues are at-least-once, so duplicates are possible) and cannot be re-read after deletion."

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: the question asks which AWS service runs mobile/browser tests on real hardware (AWS Device Farm) and what it is not built for, but the explanation is entirely about Amazon SQS long polling, ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds, and visibility timeouts. A learner reading the card gets a wrong/unrelated answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with Device Farm content, e.g.: "AWS Device Farm runs your app and Selenium/automated browser tests against real physical Android and iOS devices and real desktop browsers hosted by AWS, so you can reproduce crashes that only appear on specific hardware or OS versions, capture logs, video and performance data, and also drive devices interactively via remote access. It is not a load- or performance-testing service for your backend under real traffic (use a load-testing tool such as Distributed Load Testing on AWS), and it does not test server-side infrastructure or run arbitrary compute workloads."

findings.message: The second half of the stem, "what is it not built for", is open-ended on a free-response card: many true answers exist (backend load testing, server-side testing, production monitoring, app distribution), so a learner cannot know which negative the card expects.
findings.suggestedFix: Narrow the stem, e.g.: "Which AWS service runs those tests on real devices and browsers, and why is it the wrong choice for load-testing your backend under production-scale traffic?"

findings.message: The stem asks "Which combination of lifecycle actions...", but options c (suspend versioning), e (S3 Batch Operations job) and f (Requester Pays) are not lifecycle actions at all, so a learner can eliminate half the option set on form alone without knowing anything about versioning or multipart cleanup.
findings.suggestedFix: Either reword the stem to "Which two actions should be taken?" or replace c, e and f with genuine lifecycle configurations (e.g. an Expiration action on current versions, a NoncurrentVersionTransition to Glacier Flexible Retrieval, or a NoncurrentVersionExpiration with NoncurrentDays set to 1).

findings.message: Option f (Enable Requester Pays) is implausible for this scenario — it is a billing-attribution feature that neither removes data nor is a lifecycle action, so essentially no learner would select it.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option f with a plausible but wrong lifecycle choice, such as "Add an Expiration action that deletes current object versions 30 days after creation."
