findings.message: The support-plan requirement for the AWS Health API is stated with non-existent/incorrect plan names: AWS Support tiers are Developer, Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, and Enterprise — there is no "Unified Operations" plan, and Enterprise On-Ramp (which does grant Health API access) is omitted.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to: "the AWS Health API for programmatic polling requires a Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, or Enterprise Support plan."

findings.message: The card keys option d ("Compare published benchmark scores and pick the higher one") as correct, but that option is factually wrong as the MOST accurate basis — and its own "why" text argues against it ("Scores without cost... do not tell you dollars per solved task"). The explanation endorses measuring cost per completed task on your own tail-weighted sample, which is option a, currently marked incorrect with a null "why".
findings.suggestedFix: Set option a ("Run both on a sample weighted toward the hardest tenth of real tasks and compare dollars per successfully fixed build at each effort level.") to "correct": true, and set option d to "correct": false, keeping d's existing "why" as the rationale for why it is wrong.

findings.message: The claim that cache hits cost "0.1x (0.025x on Claude Fable 5.1)" is wrong: cache-read tokens are billed at 0.1x the model's base input price across the Claude model line, and there is no model with a 0.025x cache-read rate (no such model name exists in Anthropic's lineup).
findings.suggestedFix: Change to: "cache hits are billed at 0.1x base input price for all Claude models" and delete the parenthetical model-specific exception.

findings.message: The long-context statement is factually wrong about how the premium is applied. With the 1M-token context window, once a request's prompt exceeds 200K tokens the premium long-context rates apply to the entire request — both input and output tokens — not only to the input tokens "beyond 200K".
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with: "For requests whose prompt exceeds 200K tokens in the 1M context window, the whole request (input and output) is billed at the premium long-context rates."

findings.message: Fast mode is expressed as an absolute price ($10/$50 per million tokens) while every other modifier is a multiplier, yet the card then says cache and data-residency multipliers "stack on fast mode" without stating what base those multipliers apply to, leaving the arithmetic undefined for the learner.
findings.suggestedFix: State the fast-mode base explicitly, e.g. "fast mode replaces the base rate with $10/$50 per million tokens; cache and data-residency multipliers then apply to that fast-mode rate."

findings.message: Option c's "why" states a false SNS fact: the default delivery (retry) policy for HTTP/S endpoints is not three retries within an hour — it is 3 immediate retries, 2 pre-backoff retries, 10 backoff retries, and 100,000 post-backoff retries 20 seconds apart, spanning roughly 23 days. A learner would take away an incorrect retry figure.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "SNS pushes each notification as it arrives; with no queue in front of the workers there is nothing to absorb the spike, and an unacknowledged delivery is retried on SNS's schedule rather than left visible for another worker to claim, so a crashed worker's image is not safely handed off."

findings.message: The explanation's final sentence rebuts "Kinesis Data Streams is a replayable ordered stream, not a work queue", but no option mentions Kinesis Data Streams, so the rationale does not match the options presented.
findings.suggestedFix: Drop the Kinesis clause from the explanation, or add a Kinesis Data Streams distractor option that the clause rebuts.

findings.message: Option d begins "Keep the queue...", but the stem describes an architecture with no queue (web tier writes to S3, workers poll/resize), so the option presupposes a component that does not exist in the scenario.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword option d as: "Send S3 event notifications to an SQS queue, but scale the worker Auto Scaling group on average CPU utilization so more instances launch when the fleet is busy."

findings.message: The keyed option tells learners to set "model": "claude-3-opus-20240229", a Claude 3 Opus model ID that Anthropic deprecated and retired (retirement in early 2026), so it is no longer a usable value as of the review date; it is also inconsistent with the stem's modern "claude-sonnet-5" naming.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the value in option c with a current Opus identifier consistent with the stem, e.g. Add "model": "claude-opus-5" to .claude/settings.local.json.

findings.message: The qualifier "LEAST amount of change" does not discriminate: options a, b and d are each a single one-line edit, the same effort as the keyed option c, so another option satisfies the stated qualifier at least as well. What actually decides the answer is the scoping constraint (this repo only, no teammate impact), not the amount of change.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the qualifier and stem to the property that decides the answer, e.g. "Which approach correctly scopes the override to this developer in this repository only?" (or use a qualifier such as "LEAST impact on teammates and other projects").

findings.message: The stem's "Hint:" line is a verbatim copy of the first sentence of the explanation, and the codeSnippet already shows the object form with a "~2.1.0" semver range, so the learner is handed the entire first half of the answer (declare the dependency as an object with a version range) without needing any of the knowledge the card tests.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the "Hint:" sentence from the question, and either drop the codeSnippet or replace it with the broken pre-fix manifest (e.g. "dependencies": ["audit-logger", "secrets-vault"]) so the learner must supply the constrained object form themselves.

findings.message: Option d states exactly the same configuration as the keyed option a ("Add Read(**/.env) and Read(**/.env.*) deny rules to permissions.deny in the shared .claude/settings.json"), merely adding a runbook note, so it is at least as correct as the keyed answer and a learner cannot pick a single answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option d with the Edit-only distractor its "why" describes, e.g. "Add Edit(**/.env) and Edit(**/.env.*) deny rules to permissions.deny in the shared .claude/settings.json."

findings.message: Option d's "why" explains that Edit-only rules leave reads open, but option d's text contains Read deny rules, not Edit rules, so the rationale does not explain why that option is wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Align the "why" with the option text after rewriting option d as an Edit-only rule (the existing "why" then applies).

findings.message: The explanation's closing sentence lists the distractors as "Guidance text, a single Bash pattern and Edit-only rules", but no option as written offers Edit-only rules, so the explanation does not match the answer set.
findings.suggestedFix: Update the explanation to match the final option set (or restore the Edit-only distractor as option d).

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: the question asks why Trusted Advisor cost-optimization checks (idle EC2, underused EBS) are unavailable on the Basic support plan and what Basic does cover, but the explanation is an unrelated CloudFront vs. Global Accelerator comparison. A learner reading this card gets no correct answer and would be misled about what was asked.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with Trusted Advisor content, e.g.: "Idle EC2 instances and underutilized EBS volumes are cost-optimization checks, which require a Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, or Enterprise Support plan. On Basic and Developer plans, Trusted Advisor exposes only the core security checks (for example S3 bucket permissions, security group unrestricted ports, IAM use, MFA on root account, RDS public snapshots) plus all service quota checks. Upgrading the support plan unlocks the full five-pillar set: cost optimization, performance, security, fault tolerance, and service limits, along with programmatic access via the Trusted Advisor/Support API."

findings.message: The stem's qualifier is "MOST highly available", but the keyed option A adds a lifecycle transition to S3 Standard-IA, which is designed for 99.9% availability versus S3 Standard's 99.99% — so the keyed choice actually lowers availability, and option B (EFS Regional, also designed for 99.99% availability across multiple AZs) satisfies the availability criterion at least as well.
findings.suggestedFix: Restore the cost qualifier the card was written for: change the stem to "Which storage service is the MOST cost-effective home for this library?" and set "qualifier" to "MOST cost-effective" (or, if availability is truly the target, drop the Standard-IA lifecycle from option A and rewrite every option's "why" around availability/SLA differences).

findings.message: The explanation and realWorldUsage justify the keyed answer purely on price ("cheapest durable store", "$0.023 per GB-month", "13 times the S3 rate"), and every distractor "why" argues cost rather than availability, so nothing in the card supports the answer against the criterion the stem actually asks about.
findings.suggestedFix: Align the rationale with the stem: either restate the explanation in availability terms (S3 Standard 99.99% designed availability / 99.9% SLA, multi-AZ by default; EBS single-AZ; Glacier IR retrieval behavior) or revert the stem to the cost-optimization framing the existing explanation already supports.

findings.message: The keyed option (a) is the only one that carries its own justification clause ("so that requests signed with plain access keys, where the key is absent, are denied as well"), making it visibly longer and self-validating; a learner who does not know how aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent/BoolIfExists behaves can pick it purely from that asymmetry rather than from the tested knowledge.
findings.suggestedFix: Trim option (a) to the bare control, e.g. "Add a statement to the users' identity policies that denies ec2:TerminateInstances and s3:DeleteBucket with a BoolIfExists condition on aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent set to false." and keep the reasoning about absent keys in the explanation only.

findings.message: The code snippet sends output_config.effort with model "claude-3-opus-20240229", a Claude 3 model that has no effort support — this directly contradicts the explanation's own support list (Fable 5.1, Opus 5/4.8/4.7, Sonnet 5, partial on 4.6). The snippet also sets max_tokens 16000, which exceeds Claude 3 Opus's 4096-token output limit, so the illustrated request could never succeed.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the snippet's model to one the explanation says supports effort and use a valid max_tokens, e.g. {"model": "claude-opus-5", "max_tokens": 16000, "output_config": {"effort": "medium"}, ...}.

findings.message: claude-3-opus-20240229 is a retired model ID (Claude 3 Opus was deprecated in 2025 and reached end of life in early 2026), so as of the 2026-09-27 review date the snippet shows an API call that returns a model-not-found/retired error rather than a working example.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the retired claude-3-opus-20240229 ID with a currently supported model ID in the snippet.

findings.message: The stem asks for "the two consequences of changing effort mid-session" but the explanation names only one (changing the top-level value restarts the prompt cache); the beta per-message effort system message is an exception/workaround, not a second consequence, so the learner cannot self-check the second half of the question.
findings.suggestedFix: Either state both consequences explicitly (e.g. prompt-cache invalidation plus the change applying to all subsequent output tokens/tool-call verbosity) or reword the stem to "what is the main consequence of changing effort mid-session, and what is the beta exception?"

findings.message: Option c is verbatim the keyed option b plus a harmless extra step ("Record the change in the team's runbook"), so it is just as correct as b and a careful learner cannot choose a single answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite option c to describe a genuinely weaker scope matching its rationale, e.g. "Have each engineer add a permissions.deny rule for edits under infra/prod/ to their own user settings (~/.claude/settings.json), and record the change in the team's runbook."

findings.message: Option c's "why" argues about user settings ("depend on every engineer doing it and can be edited away"), but the option text specifies managed settings deployed to every machine, so the rationale does not explain why that option is wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Align the "why" with the revised option text, or if the option is changed to user settings, keep the existing rationale.

findings.message: Option c ("Switch to Claude Haiku 4.5 because smaller models process documents faster") offers speed as the rationale for a rejection caused by a page-count validation error, so it bears no relation to the stated failure and no learner would seriously consider it.
findings.suggestedFix: Make c a plausible near-miss, e.g. "Enable the 1M context beta header so the larger page allowance applies" (wrong because the account is already on the 1M-context model and the per-request page cap still applies), keeping the Haiku context-window detail in the 'why'.

findings.message: The explanation states a batch holds at most 10,000 requests or 32 MB; those were the original Message Batches limits but Anthropic raised them to 100,000 requests or 256 MB (whichever is reached first), so the numbers taught are no longer true as of 2026-09.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to: "A single batch holds at most 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever is hit first, so this 150,000-request / 300 MB job must be split; oversized payloads fail with 413 request_too_large."

findings.message: Option c ("Switch to the largest available model") is eliminated directly by the stem's explicit constraint "without changing the model," so no learner would select it, and its "why" never mentions that it violates the stated constraint.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option c with a plausible in-constraint control, e.g. "Add a per-ticket token/cost budget check that aborts the loop when spend exceeds a threshold" (wrong because it bounds cost but not iteration count or completion), or at minimum amend c's "why" to note it also violates the requirement not to change the model.

findings.message: The stem asks which grading method fits each of three criteria, but the explanation only maps two of them (categorical order status → code-based, tone → LLM-based); it never says how to grade "no leaked personal data," so the answer does not fully answer the question asked.
findings.suggestedFix: Add an explicit mapping for the third criterion, e.g. "Leaked personal data is string-matchable: grade it in code by scanning the output for the known PII values from the test fixture (regex/exact match), escalating to an LLM grader only for paraphrased or indirect disclosures."

findings.message: The explanation opens with the stray phrase "Ship it.", which reads as a reviewer/approval verdict rather than teaching content and is unrelated to the answer that follows (the shipping pun is not set up anywhere).
findings.suggestedFix: Delete "Ship it." and begin the explanation with "Do the arithmetic first: 500 TB is 4,000,000 gigabits...".

findings.message: "Snowball Edge Storage Optimized holds 210 TB usable" conflates two device variants: the long-standing Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device provides 80 TB usable, while 210 TB usable applies specifically to the Snowball Edge Storage Optimized 210TB (NVMe) variant. With 80 TB devices the archive would need seven devices, not three.
findings.suggestedFix: Name the variant explicitly, e.g. "Snowball Edge Storage Optimized 210TB devices provide 210 TB usable each, so three devices carry the 500 TB archive (the older 80 TB Storage Optimized device would need seven)."

findings.message: The realWorldUsage note displayed with the card states the answer outright ("answer Lake Formation rather than bucket policies") for exactly the cue in the stem ("central fine-grained permissions on the data lake" across several engines), so a learner can produce the answer without knowing the service.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword the note so it does not name the answer, e.g. "When a stem asks for central fine-grained (column/row/cell) permissions enforced across several analytics engines, think catalog-level grants rather than bucket policies or per-engine IAM."

findings.message: The qualifier is "MOST cost-effective" but the card is actually testing secure tenant isolation, and the keyed answer (server-side IDs, per-tenant workspaces, extra authorization layer) is the most operationally expensive option; the cheapest option by cost is arguably (b), a system-prompt instruction that requires no re-architecture. The keyed answer therefore does not best satisfy the stated qualifier.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the qualifier and stem to match what is being tested, e.g. "Which design correctly isolates each customer's files?" (qualifier: "MOST secure" / "correctly enforces tenant isolation"), and update the explanation wording accordingly.

findings.message: "give each tenant its own workspace" is presented as a general answer for a SaaS with "many customers," but Anthropic Console workspaces are a limited administrative resource (a fixed per-organization cap), so one workspace per tenant does not scale to many customers; the actual load-bearing control is the server-side user-to-file mapping.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword option (a) and the explanation to emphasize server-side file IDs plus your own authorization check, and mention per-tenant workspaces only as an optional extra boundary for a bounded number of tenants.

findings.message: The stem only asks which option is "an acceptable way to run this workload" and sets no cost or overhead requirement (qualifier is null), yet the explanation and the distractor rationales judge the options purely on cost. Options b, c, and d are all functionally acceptable ways to run a 3-second resize triggered by S3 uploads, so a careful learner cannot identify a single intended answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite the stem to state the deciding criterion, e.g. "Which compute option is the MOST cost-effective way to run this workload?", and set "qualifier": "MOST cost-effective".

findings.message: The explanation's closing claim ("AWS no longer offers Snow devices to new customers, yet the exam still tests this rule") directly contradicts the keyed answer, which tells the learner to order three Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices; as written the card both keys and undercuts the same action, and the availability claim is not substantiated (Snowball Edge Storage Optimized 210TB is still the Snow Family data-transfer device).
findings.suggestedFix: Remove or correct the sentence, e.g. "The Snow Family has narrowed over time (Snowmobile and Snowcone are retired); Snowball Edge Storage Optimized 210TB remains the bulk-transfer device, and the exam still tests this ship-vs-transfer rule."

findings.message: The explanation tells learners the X family (x2iedn.4xlarge, 16 vCPUs / 512 GiB) gives "the lowest cost per GiB when CPU barely matters" — which is essentially the scenario in the stem (modest CPU, 450 GiB working set) — so the supporting text partially contradicts keying the R family as the MOST cost-effective fit.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword the X-family aside to distinguish it from the stem, e.g. "X instances (x2iedn.4xlarge: 16 vCPUs, 512 GiB) drop to 32 GiB per vCPU and cost less per GiB, but they leave only 16 vCPUs — too few for a continuously busy analytics engine, so R's 8 GiB per vCPU is the better balance here."

findings.message: The stem includes S3, but Amazon S3 does not support aws:ResourceTag conditions for bucket-level actions (tag-based authorization is limited to object tags via s3:ExistingObjectTag/s3:RequestObjectTag), so the keyed option's single aws:ResourceTag/project-to-aws:PrincipalTag/project policy would not actually scope S3 access; this also contradicts the explanation's caveat that ABAC is a poor fit where a service lacks resource-tag authorization.
findings.suggestedFix: Either drop S3 from the stem (use "EC2 and RDS resources") or note in the explanation that S3 access is scoped with a per-project bucket prefix/object-tag condition (s3:ExistingObjectTag) while EC2 and RDS use aws:ResourceTag matching.

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: the question asks which IAM feature stops developers from creating roles more powerful than themselves (and why a restrictive identity policy is insufficient), but the explanation describes the pilot light disaster-recovery strategy (replication, RPO/RTO, failover). A learner gets no correct answer and is taught content unrelated to the question.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with the permissions-boundary answer, e.g.: "An IAM permissions boundary. Grant iam:CreateRole/iam:AttachRolePolicy with a Condition on iam:PermissionsBoundary requiring a specific boundary policy ARN, so any role the developer creates can never exceed the boundary's effective permissions (effective permissions = intersection of identity policy and boundary). Restricting the developer's own identity policy does not solve it because a developer who may create roles and attach policies can create a role with AdministratorAccess and assume it (or have a service assume it), escalating privileges beyond their own; the boundary constrains the created role itself, not just the creator."

findings.message: The code snippet names the tested concept outright via the condition key "iam:PermissionsBoundary", so a learner can name the feature from the code without knowing why identity-policy restrictions are insufficient. The realWorldUsage note repeats the term.
findings.suggestedFix: Either remove the codeSnippet from the front of the card (show it only with the explanation), or replace the literal key with a placeholder such as "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"iam:<condition-key>": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:policy/DevBoundary"}} and ask the learner to supply the key.

findings.message: Option e (client began logging the request-id response header) is a client-side, read-only change to a response, with no conceivable connection to the request prefix; no learner would select it, so it does no discriminating work in a choose-two item.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with a plausible near-miss, e.g. "The harness began injecting a timestamp into the last line of the system prompt on every request." — wait, that is a real invalidator; instead use something like "The client switched from streaming to non-streaming responses." with a why noting that stream/non-stream does not change the rendered prompt prefix or the cache key.

findings.message: The explanation states Lambda@Edge "runs Node.js or Python for up to 30 seconds" without qualification, but the 30-second timeout applies only to origin request/response triggers; viewer request/response triggers are limited to 5 seconds. Since option c concerns a viewer-request Lambda@Edge function, the unqualified figure can mislead.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "Lambda@Edge runs Node.js or Python with a 5-second timeout on viewer triggers and up to 30 seconds on origin triggers, can call AWS services, and also hooks origin request and origin response..."

findings.message: The qualifier "LOWEST cost" is not satisfied uniquely by the keyed answer: SCPs, per-account IAM policies (option b) and disabling Regions (option d) all cost nothing, so options b and d meet the cost qualifier at least as well as option a. The actual discriminator between the options is whether the control is preventive and administratively tamper-proof, not price.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the qualifier and stem to reflect the real discriminator, e.g. "Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?" (or "...MOST effectively prevents the action?"), and update mcq.qualifier accordingly.

findings.message: The card displays a JSON code snippet containing a `batchItemFailures` partial-batch response, which is exactly the mechanism the question tests; only option b mentions `batchItemFailures`, so a learner can match the snippet to the keyed option without knowing anything about ReportBatchItemFailures.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the codeSnippet from the question side (move the batchItemFailures JSON into the explanation only), or replace it with neutral context such as the failing handler/event source mapping configuration that does not name batchItemFailures.

findings.message: The stem ends with "Hint: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key.", which states the exact keyed answer, so the learner never has to reason about which encryption option provides per-principal CloudTrail decrypt logging and key revocation.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the "Hint: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key." line from the question; if a hint is needed, limit it to something like "Hint: consider which option gives you control over the key policy."

findings.message: The realWorldUsage advice is out of date and misstates the mechanism: S3 server access log destination buckets have supported SSE-KMS as long as an S3 Bucket Key is enabled, and when SSE-KMS is unsupported (no Bucket Key) log delivery simply fails rather than producing objects encrypted with a key you cannot read.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with: "A bucket that receives S3 server access logs can use SSE-S3, or SSE-KMS provided an S3 Bucket Key is enabled on the destination bucket; plain SSE-KMS without a Bucket Key causes log delivery to fail."

findings.message: The qualifier "MOST cost-effective" does not discriminate among the options: the keyed answer (allowed_domains + max_uses) is selected purely on security grounds, and the card's own explanation and realWorldUsage state that the token/cost control is max_content_tokens (option d), which would literally be the most cost-effective change. Judged on cost-effectiveness, option d matches the qualifier at least as well as the keyed answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the qualifier and stem to a security-effectiveness framing, e.g. qualifier "MOST effective at limiting exfiltration" and stem "...which configuration MOST effectively bounds where fetched data can go while keeping the feature?"

findings.message: The keyed option (b) is the only one that carries its own justification ("because on Foundry the model parameter is the deployment name, which only defaults to the model ID"), restating the explanation's teaching point; a learner who does not know Foundry's naming rule can pick it purely because it explains itself while the distractors are bare assertions.
findings.suggestedFix: Trim option b to a plain action, e.g. "Send the deployment name the admin chose in the Foundry portal as the model value." and keep the rationale only in the explanation.

findings.message: The explanation dismisses a distractor that does not exist on this card: "and more Lambda memory changes nothing" — there is no Lambda-memory option (a–d are usage plans, reserved concurrency, WAF rate rule, SQS queue), so the sentence will confuse learners.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete "and more Lambda memory changes nothing" from the explanation (or add a corresponding distractor option about increasing Lambda memory).

findings.message: The stated Message Batches limits are stale: Anthropic raised the per-batch cap from 10,000 requests / 32 MB to 100,000 requests / 256 MB, so as of the review date a 150,000-request batch violates a 100,000-request limit, not a 10,000-request one. The explanation's own conclusion ('150,000 needs two batches') only works under the current 100,000 limit — under the quoted 10,000 limit it would take 15 batches.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to: 'A Message Batch holds at most 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever comes first, so 150,000 requests need two batches.'

findings.message: The explanation (10,000 requests per batch) contradicts realWorldUsage ('Split into 100,000-request batches'), leaving the learner with two conflicting limits on the same card.
findings.suggestedFix: Align both fields on the current 100,000-request / 256 MB cap.

findings.message: The keyed option is the only one that carries a built-in justification clause ("so the servers' responses can return to the clients' ephemeral ports"), which hands the learner the exact concept under test (NACLs are stateless and need an explicit outbound rule for return traffic); test-wise learners can pick it without knowing NACL statefulness.
findings.suggestedFix: Trim option A to the action only, e.g. "Add an outbound allow rule to the network ACL for TCP ports 1024-65535 to 0.0.0.0/0.", and keep the reasoning in the explanation.

findings.message: Option C ("Add an inbound allow rule for TCP port 80") is implausible: the stem already states inbound 443 is allowed and that HTTPS is the failing protocol, so no port 80 rule is relevant to any reading of the scenario.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with a distractor that plausibly targets the same misconception, e.g. "Add an inbound allow rule to the network ACL for TCP ports 1024-65535 from 0.0.0.0/0" (right ephemeral range, wrong direction).

findings.message: Fargate's maximum task size is 16 vCPU with 120 GB of memory, not "32 vCPU with 244 GB"; the stated upper limit is factually wrong and would teach learners an impossible task size.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to "from 0.25 vCPU with 512 MiB up to 16 vCPU with 120 GB" (valid CPU values 256–16384, with memory tied to the chosen CPU).

findings.message: The claim of "10 GiB of ephemeral storage with no option to request more" was true only for Fargate platform versions before 1.4.0; since 2020 tasks get 20 GiB by default and ephemeralStorage can be configured up to 200 GiB.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with "20 GiB of ephemeral storage by default, configurable up to 200 GiB via the task definition's ephemeralStorage setting (platform version 1.4.0 or later)".

findings.message: Option C repeats option A's design verbatim ("Define three subagents and let them run concurrently so the review finishes in the time of the slowest check") and only adds a harmless documentation step, so it is equally correct and a learner cannot pick a single answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option C with a genuinely different, wrong design, e.g. "Use a single subagent with a larger context window to perform all three checks so the main context stays clean." — which matches the existing 'why' rationale.

findings.message: Option C's "why" ("One subagent still performs the checks one after another; window size does not create parallelism") describes a single-subagent/large-window option, not the concurrent three-subagent text actually shown, so the rationale does not explain why the option as written is wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Align the option text and its 'why' — after rewriting C as a single-subagent-with-bigger-context option, keep the current rationale.

findings.message: Option b is the keyed answer verbatim ("Save it as a skill in .claude/skills/backfill/SKILL.md with a one-line description.") plus an unrelated bookkeeping step, so it is equally correct and a learner cannot choose between a and b. Its "why" argues against putting 300 lines in CLAUDE.md, which is nothing like the option's own text, indicating the option body was replaced by a copy of option a.
findings.suggestedFix: Restore the intended distractor for b, e.g. "Append the full 300-line procedure to .claude/CLAUDE.md so it is always available.", which matches the existing rationale about CLAUDE.md loading in full every session.

findings.message: The explanation says "CLAUDE.md, an unscoped rule and a SessionStart hook all put the 300 lines into every session," but no option currently offers a CLAUDE.md approach, so the explanation refers to a choice the learner never saw.
findings.suggestedFix: After fixing option b to be the CLAUDE.md option, the explanation matches; otherwise drop the CLAUDE.md reference from the explanation.

findings.message: The stem asks which change is "acceptable" rather than which is best/most effective, so option b (adding a single example of the desired line) also qualifies as an acceptable change — its own rationale concedes it is "the right technique at the wrong dose." The stem lacks the requirement needed to rule b out.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword the stem to demand the best option, e.g. "...The team wants a consistent one-line \"category: reason\" format. Which prompt change is MOST likely to make the format consistent?"

findings.message: The explanation ends with "the distractor is an interface endpoint for S3", but this is a question-and-answer card (mcq is null) with no options, so there is no distractor; it also mildly contradicts the realWorldUsage note, since an S3 interface endpoint is the legitimate fix when access is needed over VPN/Direct Connect.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the closing clause with something like: "A common mistake is paying for an interface endpoint for S3 when the free gateway endpoint suffices for in-VPC, same-Region traffic (an S3 interface endpoint is only needed for on-premises access over VPN/Direct Connect)."

findings.message: The quoted prices ($0.045/hour and $0.045/GB for NAT Gateway, $0.01/AZ-hour and $0.01/GB for interface endpoints) are us-east-1 list prices and vary by Region, but the explanation states them as universal.
findings.suggestedFix: Qualify the figures, e.g. "in us-east-1, a NAT Gateway bills about $0.045 per hour plus $0.045 per GB processed (prices vary by Region)" and similarly for the interface endpoint rates.

findings.message: The stem gives no cost or storage-class constraint, so S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (millisecond access, no restore job) satisfies "back within minutes" at least as well as Glacier Flexible Retrieval with Expedited retrieval; the learner cannot tell which the card wants until reading the explanation.
findings.suggestedFix: Add the missing requirement to the stem, e.g. "...must be back within minutes, and you want the lowest possible storage cost that still allows minute-level restores. Which Glacier class and retrieval tier do you pick, and what does Deep Archive change?"

findings.message: The stem appends "Hint: the correct option begins \"An AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoint backed by the S3 ...\"", which names the keyed answer verbatim, so the learner never has to distinguish Transfer Family from DataSync, Storage Gateway or a self-managed EC2 SFTP server.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the hint line so the stem ends at "Which design meets this with the LEAST operational overhead?"

findings.message: The keyed answer (option b) is factually wrong: IAM identity policies cannot restrict the root user, so attaching a policy to root to limit its access keys has no effect — and option b's own "why" text says exactly that, while the explanation endorses option a's remediation. Option a (enable root MFA, delete root access keys, move the script to a least-privilege IAM role) is the correct, MOST secure answer but is keyed false.
findings.suggestedFix: Set "correct": true on option a with "why": null, and set option b to "correct": false, keeping its existing "why" rationale explaining that IAM identity policies do not constrain the root user.

findings.message: Option D repeats option B's safeguard verbatim and only adds "Record the change in the team's runbook," so it is just as correct as the keyed answer; a learner cannot choose between B and D.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option D with a genuinely wrong alternative, e.g. "Wrap each batch request in a try/except in the results-processing code and skip any entry that returns invalid_request_error." (which matches the existing 'why' about discarded errors).

findings.message: Option D's "why" ("Discarding errors hides the 30% of documents that were never processed...") describes error-swallowing behavior that appears nowhere in D's text, so it does not explain why that option is wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Align D's text and rationale — either rewrite D as an error-swallowing option or rewrite the 'why' to address what D actually proposes.

findings.message: The explanation overstates the guarantee: sts:ExternalId defends against the confused-deputy problem (a trusted vendor being tricked into acting for another tenant), but it is not a secret and gives no protection if the vendor itself is compromised, since an attacker inside the vendor's platform has the stored external IDs. Saying it stops a "compromised vendor" teaches a false security boundary.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "it stops a confused deputy — a vendor whose multi-tenant platform is tricked into using your role on behalf of another customer. It does not protect you if the vendor's own account or platform is compromised, since the external ID is not a secret."

findings.message: The card keys option B (cross-Region read replica / pilot light) as correct, but the explanation and option B's own "why" text both argue that the backup-and-restore approach in option A is the right answer for a 24-hour RPO/RTO and that the running replica wastes money. Option B is factually the wrong choice for the MOST cost-effective requirement, so the keyed answer teaches the opposite of the intended lesson.
findings.suggestedFix: Set option A ("correct": true) and option B ("correct": false), leave option B's existing "why" as its wrong-answer rationale, and set option A's "why" to null.

findings.message: The explanation misstates Lambda's payload ceilings: the asynchronous (event) invocation payload limit is 256 KB, not 1 MB (6 MB for synchronous invocation is correct).
findings.suggestedFix: Change "a 6 MB synchronous or 1 MB asynchronous payload" to "a 6 MB synchronous or 256 KB asynchronous payload".

findings.message: The explanation and option b's "why" state that Lambda is capped at 300 seconds (5 minutes). That was the limit only until October 2018; the maximum function timeout has been 900 seconds (15 minutes) since then — and the card's own summary line says "event-driven work under 15 minutes is Lambda", contradicting itself.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace "300 seconds (5 minutes)" with "900 seconds (15 minutes)" in both the explanation and option b's rationale, e.g. "A Lambda function's timeout maxes out at 15 minutes, so a 2-to-6-hour job is killed long before it finishes."

findings.message: realWorldUsage only gives advice about profiling before "committing to Lambda", which is the rejected option; it offers no practical guidance about the keyed AWS Batch / Spot answer the card actually teaches.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with a note tied to the keyed answer, e.g. "Set the Batch job definition's retry attempts and use a Spot-based managed compute environment with checkpointing to S3, so an interruption restarts from the last checkpoint instead of the beginning."

findings.message: Option c repeats the keyed answer (option a) word for word — quote-first grounding with <quotes> tags and permitted uncertainty — yet is keyed incorrect, so a learner cannot pick a single correct option. Its "why" talks about temperature/determinism, which matches no text in the option, indicating the intended distractor text was lost.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option c's text with the temperature distractor its rationale describes, e.g. "Set temperature to 0 so the model's output becomes deterministic."

findings.message: The keyed answer (and the explanation) state that a symmetric KMS key with imported key material can undergo an on-demand rotation after new material is imported. AWS KMS does not support on-demand rotation (RotateKeyOnDemand) or automatic rotation for keys whose key material origin is EXTERNAL; imported-material keys can only be rotated manually by creating a new KMS key, importing the new material into it, and repointing the alias.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword option a to: "...for the imported-material key, create a new KMS key, import the fresh material into it, and move the alias to it, keeping the old key enabled." Fix the explanation similarly: on-demand rotation is available only for symmetric encryption keys with KMS-generated key material; imported-material, asymmetric, HMAC and custom key store keys must be rotated manually.

findings.message: Option c is word-for-word identical to the keyed option a (only prefixed with "Proceed as follows:"), so two options state the same approach and a learner cannot pick a single answer. Option c's "why" also does not explain why that text would be wrong—it argues about re-encryption, which the option never mentions.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option c with a genuinely different wrong approach, e.g. "Re-encrypt all existing ciphertext under the new keys and re-sign all prior releases each year so only current keys are in use," with a why explaining that KMS retains the old key material so mass re-encryption/re-signing is unnecessary overhead.

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: the question asks about the isolation boundary for Files API uploads in a multi-tenant setup, but the explanation describes the tool_choice.disable_parallel_tool_use field, prompt cache invalidation, and programmatic tool calling. A learner is given no correct answer (and is implicitly taught that this is the answer).
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with the actual answer, e.g.: "Files uploaded via the Files API are scoped to the workspace that owns the API key, not to the individual key. All keys in the Default Workspace can list, download, and delete every tenant's files, so one API key per customer provides no isolation. Create a separate workspace per tenant (or per isolation domain) and issue that tenant's keys from it, so file IDs from one tenant are inaccessible to another."

findings.message: Option D's rationale (and the matching sentence in the explanation) asserts that an NLB's static IPs are necessarily new addresses; in fact an NLB can be created with an existing Elastic IP assigned per subnet, so the existing hard-coded address could be preserved. The distractor is still weaker than the keyed answer (it adds a load balancer and requires re-creating the NLB to move the EIP), but the stated reason is technically inaccurate.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword D's "why" to something like: "An NLB can take an Elastic IP per subnet, but standing up a load balancer and moving the address onto it is far more rework than simply reassociating the existing Elastic IP between the two instances." Adjust the explanation sentence about NLB accordingly.

findings.message: The stem ends with "Hint: the correct option begins \"Upload each screenshot once to the Files API and reference ...\"", which names the keyed option verbatim, so a learner can pick it without knowing anything about the Files API or request-size limits (and it defeats the option shuffle).
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the hint line, ending the stem at "Which change is MOST effective at keeping requests small without losing earlier screenshots?"

findings.message: The explanation inverts the semantics of the condition key: a `"Bool": {"aws:SecureTransport": "false"}` condition evaluates to true only for plain HTTP requests, not HTTPS ones. As written ("the condition is true only for HTTPS requests, so plain HTTP is rejected") the sentence is both factually wrong and self-contradictory, teaching a learner that the Deny fires on HTTPS.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "A bucket policy that denies every S3 action when aws:SecureTransport is false: that condition matches only plain HTTP requests, so HTTP is rejected by S3 itself while HTTPS passes, with nothing to run or maintain."

findings.message: The explanation's final sentence ("A bucket cannot hold an ACM certificate; S3 already terminates TLS with its own.") rebuts an option that does not exist in this MCQ — there is no ACM certificate choice — so it is leftover text that will confuse learners.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the ACM sentence, or replace it with a rebuttal tied to an actual option (e.g., expand on why the aws:SourceVpce condition in option D also adds ongoing access-management overhead).

findings.message: The stem's qualifier is "MOST highly available", but the keyed answer and every distractor rationale are argued purely on cost (per-GB vs. fixed hourly charges); a single lightly-used internet link with a single DataSync agent is not more highly available than the alternatives, so nothing in the card shows option A best satisfies the stated qualifier (the stableUid, explanation and realWorldUsage all indicate the intended qualifier was lowest cost).
findings.suggestedFix: Change the stem to "Which solution transfers the nightly data at the LOWEST cost?" and set mcq.qualifier to "MOST cost-effective", leaving the existing cost-based explanation and distractor rationales intact.

findings.message: The keyed option restates the rule being tested ("so it appears in the conversation context web fetch is allowed to use"), which pairs directly with the error_code url_not_in_prior_context in the stem; a learner who knows nothing about web fetch can match the wording and pick (a), which is also the only option carrying an explanatory justification.
findings.suggestedFix: Trim option (a) to a bare action with no rationale, e.g. "Move the URL into a user message (or a client tool result) before the request."

findings.message: Option c (Amazon Transcribe) is implausible because the stem explicitly states the tickets arrive as free text, so no learner would choose a speech-to-text service; the modality mismatch is self-evident from the stem rather than testing Comprehend knowledge.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option c with a plausible text-analysis distractor, e.g. "Call the Amazon Comprehend DetectKeyPhrases API and route tickets based on the key phrases returned" or "Use an Amazon Bedrock foundation model with a zero-shot sentiment prompt for every ticket", with a "why" explaining the higher per-ticket cost or that key phrases do not convey sentiment.

findings.message: The claim that Claude Code "adds it to your global git excludes" is inaccurate: when Claude Code creates .claude/settings.local.json it configures git to ignore it at the repository level (project .gitignore / .git/info/exclude), not in the user's global git excludes file.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "...Claude Code writes standing approvals there and configures git to ignore it for that repository (so it is never committed)."

findings.message: The explanation is entirely about AWS Lambda invocation/retry behaviour (async retries, DLQs, destinations, stream and SQS sources) and never addresses the question, which asks which federation path fits Okta SSO across dozens of accounts, a standalone account, and mobile-app end users, plus where IAM users still belong. A learner reading this card gets no correct answer to the stem.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with the federation answer, e.g.: "Dozens of accounts: AWS IAM Identity Center with Okta as the external SAML/SCIM identity provider, using permission sets assigned to accounts via AWS Organizations. One standalone account: a SAML 2.0 (or OIDC) IAM identity provider in that account with IAM roles assumed via AssumeRoleWithSAML. Mobile app customers: Amazon Cognito identity pools (web identity federation) to vend temporary credentials via AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity for scoped S3 uploads. Long-lived IAM users remain only for the rare workload that cannot use roles or federation - for example on-premises or third-party tooling that needs programmatic access keys - and should use access keys with rotation and MFA, never for human console sign-in."

findings.message: The explanation states "an object can reach 50 TB"; the maximum S3 object size is 5 TiB (~5 TB), achievable only via multipart upload. Teaching 50 TB is factually wrong by an order of magnitude.
findings.suggestedFix: Change "(an object can reach 50 TB)" to "(an object can reach 5 TiB via multipart upload, with parts of 5 MiB–5 GiB, up to 10,000 parts)".

findings.message: The explanation cites "at least 100 PUT, COPY, POST or DELETE and 300 GET or HEAD requests per second per partitioned prefix". Those were the pre-July-2018 figures; since then S3 supports at least 3,500 write and 5,500 read requests per second per partitioned prefix.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with "S3 supports at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per partitioned prefix, with no limit on the number of prefixes".

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the question at all: the stem asks about S3 Cross-Region Replication prerequisites, backfilling existing objects, and CRR's place among replication mechanisms, but the explanation describes Application Migration Service, Application Discovery Service, Migration Hub and DMS. A learner is taught nothing correct about the asked question and would be misled about what the answer is.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with S3 CRR content, e.g.: "Both the source and destination buckets must have versioning enabled, and S3 needs an IAM role that can read the source objects and replicate into the destination. CRR (a live replication rule) only applies to objects written after the rule is enabled, so objects uploaded last year are not copied; to backfill them you must run S3 Batch Replication (an S3 Batch Operations job) or copy them manually. Among AWS S3 replication mechanisms, CRR is live, asynchronous, cross-Region replication; SRR does the same within one Region; Batch Replication handles existing objects; and Multi-Region Access Points plus replication give a single global endpoint."

findings.message: The realWorldUsage note ("a FAILED status usually means the destination lost versioning or the role lacks permissions") gives away two of the things the stem asks the learner to state: that both buckets need versioning and that a replication IAM role is required.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword the note to avoid naming the prerequisites, e.g.: "After enabling a rule, check the ReplicationStatus of a few source objects; a FAILED status points at a configuration problem you can diagnose from the replication metrics and CloudTrail."
